case_name: FORCOMP Forestry Consulting Ltd. v British Columbia
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

FORCOMP Forestry Consulting Ltd. v.
British Columbia,

2019 BCSC 426

Date: 20190326

Docket:
S165177

Registry: Victoria

Between:

FORCOMP
Forestry Consulting Ltd. and Martin Watts

Plaintiffs

And:

Her
Majesty the Queen in right of the

Province of British Columbia,

Albert
Nussbaum, Jon Vivian, Patrick Martin and

Sam Otukol

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice G.R.J. Gaul

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiffs:

P.I.
Waldmann

Counsel for the Defendants Her Majesty
the Queen in right of the Province of British Columbia, Albert Nussbaum,
Jon Vivian and Patrick Martin:

A.
Dalmyn

M. Butler

Place and Date of Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

January
26 & July 3, 2018

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria,
B.C.

March
26, 2019

Introduction

[
1
]

The plaintiffs seek general, specific and
aggravated damages from the defendants for what they allege was the defendants’
malice and their intentional efforts to cause financial harm to the plaintiffs.

[
2
]

On the present application, the defendants seek
to have the plaintiffs’ pleadings struck out and their action dismissed
pursuant to Rule 9-5(1) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
. In the
alternative, the defendants seek an order that the plaintiffs deposit $20,000
with the court registry as security for the defendants’ costs and that until
this is done the plaintiffs’ action be stayed.

Background

[
3
]

The plaintiff FORCOMP Forestry Consulting Ltd.
(“FORCOMP”) is a British Columbia incorporated company. The plaintiff
Martin Watts is the principal of FORCOMP.

[
4
]

The provincial Ministry of Forests, Lands,
Natural Resource Operations & Rural Development (the “Ministry”) has a
Forest Analysis and Inventory Branch (“FAIB”).

[
5
]

The defendants Albert Nussbaum, Jon Vivian,
Patrick Martin and Sam Otukol are or were employees of FAIB.

[
6
]

Mr. Otukol has not been served with the
plaintiffs’ pleadings and consequently he has taken no part in this litigation.

[
7
]

Between 1993 and 2002, the Ministry contracted
with FORCOMP to provide forestry data analysis. Because of cuts to the Ministry’s
budget in 2002, the contract it had with FORCOMP was not renewed.

[
8
]

Mr. Watts continued to independently
examine FAIB data that the Ministry had provided to FORCOMP. This resulted in on-going
discussions and meetings with various Ministry and FAIB officials wherein Mr. Watt
expressed his concerns about the accuracy of the Ministry’s forestry data.

[
9
]

Those discussions yielded unsatisfactory results
for Mr. Watts and FORCOMP. Frustrated by the manner in which the Ministry
and FAIB had treated him and disturbed by the fact that he and FORCOMP had not
been able to secure a government contract since the spring of 2002, Mr. Watts
filed his notice of civil claim in December 2016.

[
10
]

In the spring of 2017 the defendants applied pursuant
to Rule 9-5(1) for an order striking the plaintiffs’ pleadings and dismissing
the plaintiffs’ action. In reasons indexed at
2017 BCSC 1157
, Master Bouck
granted much of the relief the defendants were seeking and struck out practically
all of the plaintiffs’ notice of civil claim. At paras. 12-14 of her
reasons, Master Bouck explained:

[12]

When the NOCC is read as a whole, it is plain and obvious to this
presider that all of the plaintiffs’ claims as pled are bound to fail at trial.

[13]

What then is the proper result? The NOCC cannot be left to stand in
its present form. Nonetheless, the plaintiffs ought to be given an opportunity
to properly plead their case. The difficulty is that the NOCC is so flawed that
any amendments will be essentially a re-write of the entire pleading, save and
except the identification of the parties. While it is tempting to perform a
more precise analysis of the NOCC in these reasons in order to clearly
delineate the expectations of the court with respect any new NOCC, such an
exercise would essentially put the court in the position of drafting the
plaintiffs’ pleading. By virtue of these reasons, the plaintiffs have been told
that the Crown’s objections to the NOCC are legitimate. It behooves the
plaintiffs to present a pleading that addresses all of the defects and
omissions identified by the Crown and this court. In doing so, the plaintiffs
should be also mindful of putting forward a pleading that is concise and
otherwise conforms to the requirements of
SCCR
3-7.

[14]

Accordingly, save for the style of cause and
paragraphs 1 through 4 under Part 1 (statement of facts), the NOCC is
struck in its entirety, with liberty to the plaintiffs to file an amended
notice of civil claim on or before August 31, 2017.

[
11
]

Master Bouck also ordered that the plaintiffs pay the defendants’
costs, fixed at $750.

Basis of the Plaintiffs’ Claims

[
12
]

The plaintiffs filed an amended notice of civil
claim on 30 August 2017. In Part 1 – Statement of Facts, the plaintiffs
allege that:

…

5.         FAIB’s public function was to
develop and maintain forestry data and to provide services to the Ministry and
to the forestry community, including providing data for industry and compliance
purposes …

6.         FORCOMP has expertise in growth
and yield modeling, software development, statistics, data management, data
analysis and data validation. Its business requires information and data
developed, maintained and provided by the Ministry.

7.         Watts has extensive experience
and qualifications in forestry. Watts has a M.Sc. in Forestry, is a Registered
Professional Forester with the Association of B.C. Forest Professionals and an
Environmental Professional …

8.         The Ministry maintains as part of
its public obligations forest growth models including the Variable Density
Yield Projection – version 7 (“VDYP7”) for natural (existing) stands, and the
Tree and Stand Simulator (“TASS”) for managed (future) stands. Public access to
TASS yields are provided through the Table Interpolation Program for Stand
Yield (“TIPSY”) software.

9.         Beginning in 1997, FORCOMP
provided services to FAIB to prepare permanent sample plot (“PSP”) data to
calibrate VDYP7 coined as the ‘enhanced data validation’ project. In 2002, FAIB
ended the enhanced data validation project due to budget cuts.

10.       Since the 2002 budget cuts, Watts
has been pointing out problems to FAID in the FAIB data management, compilation
and analysis that caused undocumented uncertainty and errors associated with
FAIB forest growth models and biomass conversion equations. Watts identified
serious deficiencies in FAIB data and analysis and continued to point out
defects in the Ministry’s handling and integrity of forest data from 2002 to
2015. Some deficiencies that Watts identified which have led to significant
errors in forest and resource planning …

11.       FAIB and the individual defendants
knew that the deficiencies and errors identified by Watts had potentially
harmful effects on the integrity of the forestry oversight system. They also
knew that ignoring these errors was contrary to their public obligations. FAIB
and the individual defendants were embarrassed by Watts’ exposure of these
errors and were resentful of Watts. As a result, FAIB and the individual
defendants had malice towards Watts and intended to harm him.

12.       FAIB and the individual defendants
used their offices with the intention of causing harm to Watts as a reprisal
for Watts’ expression of speech identifying their errors.

13.       Between 2002 and 2014, all four
aforementioned FAIB employees agreed among themselves to exclude Watts and FORCOMP
from subsequent bidding processes and contracts with the Ministry and from
having needed forestry data by

a.         setting
contract bidding qualifications that they knew Watts and FORCOMP could not
satisfy in order to eliminate Watts and FORCOMP from the bidding process;

b.         rejecting
FORCOMP and Watts from the FAIB list of pre-qualified contractors in 2011 –
2014, a list identical in all material respects to previous years when FORCOMP
was approved;

c.         denying
access to FORCOMP and Watts to data and information that are routinely and
regularly provided to other contractors; and

d.         interfering
in contracts between FORCOMP and other government branches.

14.       At all material times the Ministry
had the following legal obligations and duties which were all violated by
publishing and relying on incorrect data and data analysis:

(a)        to
consider the rate of timber production that may be sustained on an area taking
into account the composition of the forest and its expected rate of growth in
determining an allowable annual cut pursuant to
s. 8(8)
of the
Forest
Act
, RSBC 1996 c. 157;

(b)        to
manage, protect and conserve government forest and range resources pursuant to

section 4
(b) of the
Ministry of Forests and Range Act
, RSBC 1996,
c. 300;

(c)        to plan
the use of government forest and range resources in consultation and
cooperation with the private sector pursuant to
section 4
(c) of the
Ministry
of Forests and Range Act
, RSBC 1996, c. 300; and

(d)        to
ensure practices that promote fair and open procurement, competition, demand
aggregation, value for money, transparency and accountability pursuant to
section 3(c) of the
Procurement Services Act
, SBC c. 22 and the
Core
Policy and Procedure Manual
.

15.       In order to harm Watts, FAIB and
the individual defendants were prepared to violate their public obligations described
in para. 14 above and cause harm to Watts to prevent him from exposing and
giving voice to their deficiencies. The Defendants did this with malice towards
Watts, and knowing their actions were contrary to their public obligations,
particularly as they were aware of Watts’ expressed concerns with FAIB’s data
were correct.

16.       Defendants Otukol and Martin were
at material times responsible for setting bidding process qualifications form
which FORCOMP was disqualified. Otukol rejected FORCOMP from the FAIB 2011 –
2014 list of qualified contractors even though FORCOMP had been approved in the
prior identified list.

17.       In or around 2005, Vivian
influenced another Ministry branch to stop a potential contract it had with FORCOMP.

18.       On December 17, 2014, Nussbaum
confirmed in writing to Watts that FAIB would not deal with Watts and implicitly
FORCOMP.

19.       In or around November 2016, Watts
and a colleague were invited to make a presentation at a 2017 Coastal
Silviculture Committee workshop. Nussbaum contacted the organizers and tried to
have Watts’ invitation rescinded to harm Watts.

20.       Prior to 2002, FORCOMP had annual
income from FAIB contracts since 1993 of up to $132,000. From April 2002 and on
FORCOMP has not been awarded any contracts with FAIB and his income form others
in the forestry community has diminished severely.

21.       As FAIB and its conduct is central
to the BC forestry community, knowledge of FAIB’s treatment of Watts and FORCOMP
is generally known in this specialized community. Since the dispute between
FAIB and Watts, BC forestry industry members have avoided doing business with FORCOMP
and Watts, effectively causing the Plaintiffs to be alienated from the forestry
industry community.

22.       Watts and FORCOMP’s profitability
and reputation have been destroyed in the period from 2002 to 2014 due to the
actions of the Defendants

23.       As a
result of the Defendants’ actions, Watts can no longer obtain reasonable
employment or contracts within his field to effect his livelihood.

[
13
]

On 19 September 2017, counsel for the defendants sent counsel for
the plaintiffs a letter enclosing a formal Demand for Particulars. The
plaintiffs provided their response on 24 October 2017.

[
14
]

The relief the plaintiffs seek in their amended notice of civil
claim is essentially the same as that sought in their original pleadings. As I
read the amended pleadings and the plaintiffs’ responses to the defendants’
demand for particulars, the plaintiffs’ claim can be sorted into four
categories:

a)

Misfeasance in public office;

b)

Conspiracy;

c)

Breach of the plaintiffs’ freedom of expression
as guaranteed under
s. 2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
; and

d)

The tort of “Blacklisting”.

[
15
]

In Part 3 of the amended notice of civil claim, the plaintiffs
explain the “Legal Basis” of each of the four categories.

[
16
]

“Misfeasance in public office” is addressed as follows:

26.       The FAIB employees, and by
extension the Ministry, committed misfeasance in public office in that they
deliberately used their positions of power to cause damage to the Plaintiffs
knowing that the Plaintiffs would probably be harmed.

…

29.       All four aforementioned FAIB
employees made decisions contrary to their legal obligations above and in so
doing behaved in an unlawful manner in that they ignored and exacerbated the
problems with the forestry data identified and raised by Watts. These
deficiencies in data have substantially degraded the attainment and viability
of the function of FAIB.

30.       Defendants Otukol and Martin, who
were responsible for deciding and setting bidding qualifications, intentionally
set qualifications eliminating FORCOMP and Watts from contract opportunities
with FAIB.

31.       The FAIB employees, as public
officers with training and experience, knew that their decisions would
undermine the Plaintiff’s (sic) livelihood.

32.       The FAIB employees’ acts were
deliberate, reckless or motivated by a desire to frustrate and undermine FORCOMP
and Watts’ business.

33.       The FAIB employees’ acts amount to
deliberate, unlawful conduct done in the exercise of public functions and that
they were aware that their conduct was unlawful and likely to injure FORCOMP
and Watts.

34.       Because of the FAIB employees’
acts in sabotaging the Plaintiffs’ opportunities to do business with the
Ministry, the Plaintiffs have been deprived of profits and other opportunities
within the forestry community.

35.       The
damages suffered by FORCOMP and Watts are consequences which the Defendants
knew would result from their wrongful conduct in undermining FORCOMP and Watts.

[
17
]

The claim founded on “conspiracy” is described as follows:

38.       The four aforementioned FAIB
employees conspired against FORCOMP and Watts by agreeing sometime in 2002 to
2014 to exclude Watts and FORCOMP from contract opportunities and ensuring that
Watts and FORCOMP would not meet bidding qualifications on government contracts
and was eliminated from the list of qualified contractors. These agreements
were done to hinder Watts and FORCOMP from exposing the deficiencies in FAIB’s
function of generated (sic) and distributing useful data fro the purposes of
forest management.

39.       Despite being told to stop
criticizing the Ministry, Watts continued to point out errors to the
embarrassment of FAIB and the four individual Defendants.

40.       The
FAIB employees intended to cause damage to FORCOMP and Watts by depriving them
of contracts and opportunities and damaging their reputation, which are all
consequences that the defendants knew would follow from their actions and
agreement.

[
18
]

During the course of his submissions, counsel
for the plaintiffs pointed to paragraphs 39 and 40 of the amended notice of
civil claim as also being a part of the plaintiffs’ claim based on a breach of

s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
. This facet of the plaintiffs’ claim is
further described as follows:

43.       The Supreme Court of Canada
majority and dissent in
Ernst v. Alberta Energy Regulator
held that
where there are allegations that actions of a public body are punitive,
arbitrary, and retaliatory, the allegations are sufficient to establish that
the functions of vindication and deterrence could be supported by an award of
Charter

damages.

44.       The
Defendants violated the Plaintiffs’
section 2(b)

Charter
rights. Their
decisions and actions were intended to punish Watts for openly criticizing the
Ministry, thereby limiting his freedom of expression.

[
19
]

The final and novel claim of “Blacklisting” is
addressed in the amended notice of civil claim as follows:

52.       The Court should recognize
blacklisting contractors in unique fields as a nominate tort.

…

54.       There are no other torts that
provide adequate remedy to plaintiffs in FORCOMP and Watts’ position.

…

58.       A tort of blacklisting could
require the plaintiff to show:

a.         the
defendant has public, statutory or common law obligations to be fair to the
plaintiff;

b.         proof
of malice by the defendant which is the partial or predominant cause of the
defendant refusing or refusing to continue to employ or contract with the
plaintiff;

c.         that
the plaintiff as a result is unable to retain reasonable employment or
contracts within his field to effect his livelihood; and

d.         damages
or loss suffered as a result.

…

61.       The FAIB employees intentionally
and maliciously diminished Watts’ liberty to work and continue his business in
the BC forestry industry by irreparably damaging Watts and FORCOMP’s reputation.
FAIB refused to continue contracting with FORCOMP and Watts and caused other
groups and government branches to refuse working with FORCOMP and Watts.

62.       Otukol
rejected FORCOMP from the FAIB 2011 – 2014 list of qualified contractors even
though FORCOMP had been approved in the prior identical 2007 – 2011 list.

The Application

[
20
]

The defendants are before the court again seeking, pursuant to Rule
9-5(1), an order striking the whole of the notice of civil claim and dismissing
the plaintiffs’ action.

[
21
]

In the alternative, the defendants seek an order compelling the
plaintiffs to provide security for the defendants’ costs before proceeding to
trial. The plaintiffs are not opposed to such an order on the condition that
they are given 60 days to comply with the order.

Position of the Defendants

[
22
]

The defendants argue that the four facets of the plaintiffs’ claim
fail to disclose any reasonable cause of action. Additionally, the defendants
contend that the plaintiffs’ pleadings again fail to comply with the
Rules
,
especially Rule 3-7. The defendants assert that the pleadings, including the
additional particulars that the plaintiff provided in response to the demand
for further particulars, are “prolix, unresponsive, indecipherable, confusing
and [do] not assist the defendants in discerning the case to be met.” As such
the defendants allege the pleadings are unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious and
amounts to an abuse of process.

Position of the Plaintiffs

[
23
]

The plaintiffs maintain they have heeded the words of Master Bouck
and have now properly and specifically articulated and particularized all
facets of their claim against the defendants. Furthermore, the plaintiffs argue
that the defendants now have or should have a clear and firm grasp of the
nature of the case they need to meet. In other words, the plaintiffs say their
amended pleadings, supplemented by the additional particulars that have been
provided, now disclose a reasonably founded claim that is not frivolous,
vexatious or an abuse of the court’s process.

The Law

[
24
]

Rule 3-1(2) sets out what a notice of civil
claim must contain:

(2)  A notice of civil claim must do the
following:

(a) set out a concise statement of the material facts giving rise to
the claim;

…

(g) otherwise comply
with Rule 3-7.

[
25
]

Rule 3-7 reads:

(1)  A pleading must
not contain the evidence by which the facts alleged in it are to be proved.

…

(9)  Conclusions of law must not be pleaded unless the material facts
supporting them are pleaded.

…

(17)
It is sufficient to allege malice, fraudulent intention, knowledge
or other condition of the mind of a person as a fact, without setting out the
circumstances from which it is to be inferred.

(18)  If the party pleading relies on misrepresentation, fraud, breach of
trust, wilful default or undue influence, or if particulars may be necessary,
full particulars, with dates and items if applicable, must be stated in the
pleading.

(19)  If the particulars required under subrule (18) of debt, expenses or
damages are lengthy, the party pleading may refer to this fact and, instead of
pleading the particulars, must serve the particulars in a separate document
either before or with the pleading.

(20)
Particulars need only be pleaded to the extent that they are known
at the date of pleading, but further particulars

(a)
may be served after they become
known, and

(b)
must be served within 10 days
after a demand is made in writing.

…

(22)  The
court may order a party to serve further and better particulars of a matter
stated in a pleading.

(23)  Before applying to the court for particulars, a party must demand
them in writing from the other party.

(24)  A demand for particulars does not
operate as a stay of proceedings or give an extension of time, but a party may
apply for an extension of time for serving a responding pleading on the ground
that the party cannot answer the originating pleading until particulars are
provided.

[
26
]

Rule 9-5 governs applications to strike out
pleadings. The Rule provides, in part, that:

(1)  At any stage of a
proceeding, the court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any
part of a pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)  it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)  it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)  it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing
of the proceeding, or

(d)  it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceedings to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application paid as special costs.

[
27
]

While the defendants have cited each of the four
grounds as a basis upon which the plaintiffs’ pleadings can be struck, they
place the greatest focus and emphasis on (a), (b) and (d).

[
28
]

The threshold the defendants must meet is a high
one. An application to strike pleadings must be used carefully and the court
should consider the merits of such an application by adopting a broad view that
includes “[erring] on the side of permitting a novel but arguable claim to
proceed to trial.” (See:
R. v.

Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.
,
2011
SCC 42
at para.
21
).

[
29
]

With respect to Rule 9-5(1)(a), Madam Justice
Fisher helpfully explained in
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC 1083
that:

[18]      The
test for striking a claim as disclosing no reasonable claim under Rule
9-5(1)(a), set out in
Hunt v Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 SCR 959 and
reiterated more recently in
R. v Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.
,
2011 SCC
42
, is whether it is "plain and obvious," assuming the facts pleaded
are true, that the claim discloses no reasonable cause of action, has no
reasonable prospect of success, or if the action is "certain to
fail." If there is a chance that the plaintiffs might succeed, then they should
not be "driven from the judgment seat." No evidence is admissible on
an application under Rule 9‑5(1)(a).

[
30
]

Rule 9-5(2) provides that no evidence is admissible on an
application under Rule 9-5(1)(a). Consequently an application to strike based
on the assertion that the pleadings disclose no reasonable claim must proceed
on the presumption that the facts pleaded in the notice of civil claim are
true, unless they are “manifestly incapable of being proven” (see:
Imperial
Tobacco
at para. 22).

[
31
]

The defendants also seek to strike the
plaintiffs’ pleadings because they are said to be unnecessary, frivolous,
embarrassing, vexatious and scandalous. That is, they breach Rule 9‑5(1)(b).
Justice Fisher addressed this portion of the Rule in
Willow

and concluded:

[20]      Under Rule
9-5(1)(b), a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff's cause of action, if it does not advance any claim
known in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it
would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the court's time and
public resources:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish
Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ No. 2160 (SC);
Skender v Farley
,
2007 BCCA
629
. If a pleading is so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is
pleaded, it may also be unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious. An application
under this sub-rule may be supported by evidence.

[
32
]

In the more recent decision of
The Public
Guardian and Trustee of British Columbia v. Johnston
,
2016 BCSC 1388
,
aff’d
2017 BCCA 59
, Madam Justice Balance examined Rule 9-5(1)(b) and
observed:

[52]      A pleading may be embarrassing or
scandalous within the contemplation of the Rule where it: does not state the
real issues in an intelligible form; is overly prolix; includes irrelevant
facts; is calculated to confuse the opposing party and make it difficult, and
perhaps impossible, to answer; or contains arguments or evidence:
Kuhn v.
American Credit Indemnity Co.
,
[1992] B.C.J. No. 953 (S.C.)
;
McNutt
v. A.G. Canada et al.
,
2004 BCSC 1113
at para.
41
;
B.C./Yukon
Association of Drug War Survivors v. Abbotsford (City)
,
2014 BCSC 1817
at paras.
93-94
;

Spillane v. United Parcel Service Canada Ltd. et al
,
2006 BCSC 687

at para.
22
;
Budgell v. British Columbia
,
2007 BCSC 991
at para.
20
.

[53]      That
being said, so long as the pleadings do not confuse the opposing party or make
it difficult for that party to understand the case that must be met, sheer
verbosity does not ordinarily provide sufficient justification for striking a
claim:
Doyle
at para. 4;
347202 B.C. Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial
Bank of Commerce
,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 449 (S.C.)
;
Stanley v. KCL West
Holdings Inc. et al
,
2004 BCSC 1555
.

[
33
]

As a final ground justifying the relief sought,
the defendants submit that the plaintiffs’ pleadings and action as a whole
amount to an abuse of process. Justice Fisher addressed this ground as
well in
Willow
at para.
21
where she remarked:

[21]      Abuse
of process under Rule 9-5(1)(d) or the court's inherent discretion is a
flexible doctrine. It allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding where
to do so would violate principles of judicial economy, consistency, finality
and the integrity of the administration of justice. A claim may be struck where
it is a collateral attack on an administrative decision that is subject to
appeal or judicial review:
Cimaco International Sales Inc. v British
Columbia
,
2010 BCCA 342
;
Stephen v HMTQ
,
2008 BCSC 1656
;
Varzeliotis
v British Columbia
,
2007 BCSC 620
;
Gemex Developments Corp. v City of
Coquitlam
,
2002 BCSC 412
;
Berscheid v Ensign
,
1999 CanLII 6494 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ No. 1172
(SC). A claim may also be struck as an abuse of process where it is an attempt
to re-litigate an issue that has already been decided:
Toronto (City) v
Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE), Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
.

Discussion

Is there a
“Reasonable Claim” disclosed in the Plaintiffs’ Pleadings?

[
34
]

The first aspect of the
claim advanced by the plaintiffs is misfeasance in public office. The essence
of the complaint is that the Ministry and the identified FAIB employees
intentionally altered the list of necessary qualifications so as to restrict FORCOMP’s
ability to access forestry data and thus eliminate the plaintiffs from
competing for and obtaining forestry contract work with the Province. In other
words, the defendants deliberately chose to use their powers and authority as
public servants to cause financial harm to the plaintiffs.

[
35
]

In
J.P. v. British
Columbia (Children and Family Development)
,
2017 BCCA 308
, Madam
Justice Smith explained that the tort of misfeasance in public office:

[321]    … is based
on the premise that those who hold public office may not exercise their power
in a deliberate and unlawful manner for the ulterior or improper purpose of
harming a member of the public. The rationale for the tort was articulated by
Lord Steyn in
Three Rivers D.C. v. Bank of England
, [2000] W.L.R. 1220
at 1230 (U.K.H.L.): "... in a legal system based on the rule of law
executive or administrative power 'may be exercised only for the public good'
and not for ulterior and improper purposes."

[322]    In
Odhavji
Estate v. Woodhouse
,
2003 SCC 69
at para.
30
, the Court explained the
rationale of the tort as "to protect each citizen's reasonable expectation
that a public officer will not intentionally injure a member of the public
through
deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions.
"

[323]    For good
reason, the ambit of the tort has always been narrow. As was observed by Madam
Justice Newbury in
Powder Mountain Resorts Ltd. v. British Columbia
,

2001 BCCA 619
:

[2] But for
reasons that are perhaps obvious, the tort must be used cautiously. Otherwise,
the courts risk straying into the arena of political decision-making, bypassing
the normal restraints associated with judicial review, and becoming the
arbiters of the personal thought processes of public officials. One recent
commentator (Phillip Allott, "EC Directives and Misfeasance in Public
Office", [2000] 59
Camb. L.J.
4) has written that the court should
not, by means of the tort, take on the role of "ombudsman, a parliamentary
committee, or an organ of public opinion in reviewing even egregious acts of
maladministration, official incompetence, or bad judgement." (at 6.) To
avoid dangers of this kind, a balance must be sought between curbing unlawful
behaviour on the part of governmental officials on the one hand, and on the
other, protecting officials who are charged with making decisions for the
public good, from unmeritorious claims by persons adversely affected by such
decisions. ...

[324]    There are
two branches of the tort; both share two common elements: (1)
deliberate
unlawful conduct by a public officer in the exercise of his or her powers (the
actus
reus
); and (2) the awareness (knowledge) that the unlawful conduct is
likely to injure the particular plaintiff (the
mens rea
)
:
Odhavji

at para. 23. With respect to the nature of the conduct, "
the
essential question to be determined is not whether the officer has unlawfully
exercised a power actually possessed, but whether the alleged misconduct is
deliberate and unlawful"
:
Odhavji
at para. 24.

[325]    The two
ways this tort can arise were first described by the House of Lords in
Three
Rivers
and subsequently adopted by the Supreme Court in
Odhavji
:

[22] ... In
Three
Rivers
, the House of Lords held that the tort of misfeasance in a public
office can arise in one of two ways, what I shall call Category A and Category
B. Category A involves conduct that is specifically intended to injure a person
or class of persons. Category B involves a public officer who acts with
knowledge both that she or he has no power to do the act complained of and that
the act is likely to injure the plaintiff.

[326]    Category A
misfeasance is established when a public officer exercises his or her power for
the specific purpose of harming the plaintiff.
Three Rivers
described it
as
"targeted malice" that includes conduct done for the ulterior
or improper purpose of harming the plaintiff
. Proof of the specific intent
to harm the plaintiff will be sufficient to establish that the public officer
had knowledge his or her conduct was likely to harm the plaintiff:
Odhavji

at para. 23.

[327]    Category B
misfeasance is more complex. It does not require a finding of specific intent
to harm the plaintiff, but rather an objective determination that
the public
officer knowingly engaged in a deliberate unlawful act with an awareness that
his or her conduct would likely harm the plaintiff or a class of plaintiffs.

Knowledge of harm alone is insufficient to establish that the public officer
acted in bad faith or dishonestly. Rather,
the officer must know that the
deliberate conduct is inconsistent with the obligations of the office,
including that it exceeds the powers of the office, or omits a legally required
act
:
Odhavji
at para. 28 and
Powder Mountain
at para. 67.

[328]    Thus, to
establish Category B misfeasance, the mother was required to prove that Mr. Strickland
deliberately engaged in an unlawful act, knowing of the possible harmful
consequences to her and the children, and she was required to prove each
element of the tort independently of the other:
Odhavji
at para. 23.

[329]    The mental
element of Category A or Category B misfeasance establishes the "bad
faith" or "dishonesty" of the public officer. Accordingly, it
requires "clear proof commensurate with the seriousness of the
wrong":
Powder Mountain
at para. 8 and
Odhavji
at para. 28.

Awareness or knowledge that the unlawful act is likely to harm the plaintiff
requires at least a subjective recklessness or wilful blindness, if not actual
knowledge, of the likely consequences of the unlawful act
:
Powder Mountain

at paras. 7 and
Odhavji
at paras. 25 and 38.
Subjective
recklessness or wilful blindness requires a higher standard of proof than
objective foreseeability of harm for negligence. The mental element of the tort
thus constrains its ambit from including inadvertent or negligent conduct by a
public officer in the discharge of his or her official obligations
:
Odhavji

at para. 26.

[Emphasis added.]

[
36
]

In asserting that the
claim of misfeasance in public office has been properly and sufficiently
pleaded, the plaintiffs rely on both the “Statement of Facts” found in Part 1
and the “Legal Basis” found in Part 3 of the amended notice of civil claim.

[
37
]

The plaintiffs allege Mr. Watts
pointed out serious and continuing errors and defects in the Ministry’s forestry
data collection and analysis. In doing so he embarrassed and upset Ministry
officials. According to Mr. Watts, some or all of these officials, at
various ill-defined times, changed the qualifications required to compete for
Ministry and FAIB contracts; intentionally refused to award contracts to
FORCOMP; refused to give Mr. Watts the forestry data that they were providing
to others; and interfered with contracts or contractual negotiations the
plaintiffs were engaged in with other government departments. All of this
improper conduct, say the plaintiffs, was designed to financially hurt and
cripple them.

[
38
]

I have read the entirety of the amended notice
of civil claim. Additionally I have examined the plaintiffs’ response to the
demand for particulars. Finally, I have considered the draft “Amended
Plaintiffs’ Response to Demand for Particulars of the Defendants” that is
attached as an appendix to the plaintiffs’ Application Response. In their
Response the plaintiffs explain the purpose of this latter document as follows:

20.       The
defendants demanded particulars and received them, but complain they are too
detailed and contain evidence. The plaintiffs have attached as an Appendix a
draft simplified amended Response to Particulars to satisfy the defendants with
the information available to the plaintiffs at this time, in keeping with the
requirements under Rule 3-7(20).

[
39
]

The examination of the
plaintiffs’ pleadings entailed a detailed and at times cumbersome exercise of having
to sift through the plaintiffs’ pleadings to determine the material facts they
say support their claim. Having done so I can say that much of what is
contained in the plaintiffs’ pleadings is speculation, expressions of sentiment,
or conclusory statements. In other words, to a great extent the pleadings are
nothing more than an expansive fishing expedition.

[
40
]

I am not convinced that
the plaintiffs have pleaded the material facts that, if presumed to be true,
would amount to a reasonable claim that the defendants or any of them engaged
in any deliberately unlawful conduct in the exercise of the employment duties
that they knew or ought to have known would result in tangible harm to the
plaintiffs.

[
41
]

In my opinion, the
plaintiffs’ claim founded on misfeasance in public office, as pleaded, has no
reasonable prospect of success and is bound to fail.

[
42
]

The second claim being
advanced by the plaintiffs is one of conspiracy. The essence of this claim is
that the defendants colluded amongst themselves to deprive the plaintiffs of
the opportunity to compete for employment contracts with the Provincial
Government.

[
43
]

In
311165 BC Ltd. v.
Canada (Attorney General)
,
2016 BCSC 2068
, varied in part on other grounds,

2017 BCCA 196
, Mr. Justice Masuhara examined the legal principles relating
to civil conspiracy and remarked:

[53]      There are
two types of conspiracy in tort law: predominant purpose conspiracy and
unlawful means conspiracy:
Pro-Sys Consultants Ltd. v. Microsoft Corporation
,

2013 SCC 57
at para.
73
.

[54]

The elements of predominant purpose conspiracy are:
(1) an agreement or concerted action between two or more persons; (2) with the
predominant purpose of causing injury to the plaintiff; and (3) overt acts
committed that cause damage to the plaintiff:
Watson v. Bank of America
Corporation
,
2015 BCCA 362
at para.
125
.

[55]      Like
predominant purpose conspiracy, unlawful means conspiracy requires an agreement
or concerted action between two or more persons. The additional elements of
unlawful means conspiracy are that: (1) the conduct of the defendants is
unlawful; (2) the conduct is directed towards the plaintiff (alone or with
others); (3) the defendants should know that injury to the plaintiff is likely
to result; and (4) injury to the plaintiff does occur:
Watson
at para.
56
.

[56]      Pleadings
alleging conspiracy must be as specific as possible:
Can-Dive Services Ltd.
v. Pacific Coast Energy Corp.

(1993),
1993 CanLII 6870 (BC CA)
,
96 B.C.L.R. (2d) 156
at para.
9

(C.A.)
, leave to appeal ref'd [1993] S.C.C.A. No. 159, [1993] 3 S.C.R.
viii (note).
In
Can-Dive Services Ltd.
at para.
8
, Chief Justice
McEachern quoted with approval the following excerpt from J.I.H. Jacob &
Iain S. Goldrein, eds.,
Bullen & Leake & Jacob's Precedents of
Pleadings
, 13th ed. (London, U.K.: Sweet & Maxwell, 1990) at 221-22:

The statement of
claim should describe who the several parties to the conspiracy are and their
relationship with each other. It should allege the conspiracy between the
defendants giving the best particulars it can of the dates when or dates
between which the unlawful conspiracy was entered into or continued, and the
intent to injure ... It should state precisely the objects and means of the
alleged conspiracy to injure and the overt acts which are alleged to have been
done by each of the alleged conspirators in pursuance of the conspiracy, and
lastly, the injury and damage occasioned to the plaintiff ...

[
44
]

The plaintiffs argue
that a conspiracy is not typically forged and committed in public. By its
nature a conspiracy is secretive. For this reason they say all that they can
allege is that there must have been agreement between the defendants or some of
them to restrict his access to forestry data that others were receiving and
eventually ostracize Mr. Watts from the Ministry and the general forest
industry.

[
45
]

Although the plaintiffs do not clearly articulate in their amended
notice of civil claim whether they are alleging “predominant purpose”
conspiracy or “unlawful means” conspiracy, it would appear that they favour the
former. Irrespective of which it is, I am not convinced the material facts
alleged by the plaintiffs identify either type of conspiracy. The allegations
are vague and undefined. They span a period of time greater than ten years and
do not clearly identify who is alleged to have done what, with whom and when,
to conceive and implement the alleged conspiracy.

[
46
]

In my view it is plain and obvious that the plaintiffs’ pleadings
for the claim based on the tort of conspiracy disclose no reasonable cause of
action.

[
47
]

The plaintiffs’ third claim is founded upon an
alleged breach of
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
, which reads:

2. Everyone has the following
fundamental freedoms:

…

(
b
) freedom
of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and
other media of communication;

…

[
48
]

Mr. Watts says the plaintiffs were deliberately punished by the
defendants because of his continued efforts to publicize and address what he
considered was incorrect and misleading data emanating from the Ministry and
FAIB. That retribution included the defendants’ concerted efforts to intentionally
limit his opportunities to speak publicly about his concerns. Moreover, the
plaintiffs contend the defendants embarked on a course of conduct that was
designed to silence them by hurting their financial viability. As counsel for
the plaintiffs explained in his submission, “the defendants’ purpose was to
stop Mr. Watts from expressing the truth and they have been successful in
destroying his business”. Counsel added, the defendants’ attitude amounted to
“if you are going to criticize the government, we will hurt you”.

[
49
]

Having conducted my review and assessment of the pleadings as
supplemented by the plaintiffs’ response to the demand for particulars, I fail
to see how, even if all of the alleged facts are taken as true, those facts
amount to a legitimate cause of action founded on
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

[
50
]

Like the findings I made with respect to the plaintiffs’ claim based
on misfeasance in public office and the claim based on conspiracy, I accept the
defendants’ argument that there is no reasonable cause of action based on

s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
articulated in the plaintiffs’ pleadings and
that what is there is certain to fail were it to go to trial.

[
51
]

The final claim being pursued by the plaintiffs
is one that they acknowledge is novel and not currently know to the common law.
That is, the tort of “Blacklisting”. In support of their argument that their
pleadings are appropriate and that this is a reasonable and viable claim, the
plaintiffs rely on the following observations of Chief Justice McLachlin
in
Imperial Tobacco
:

[21]      Valuable
as it is, the motion to strike is a tool that must be used with care. The law
is not static and unchanging. Actions that yesterday were deemed hopeless may
tomorrow succeed. Before
Donoghue
v. Stevenson
,
1932 CanLII 536 (FOREP)
, [1932] A.C. 562 (H.L.) introduced
a general duty of care to one's neighbour premised on foreseeability, few would
have predicted that, absent a contractual relationship, a bottling company
could be held liable for physical injury and emotional trauma resulting from a
snail in a bottle of ginger beer. Before
Hedley
Byrne & Co. v. Heller & Partners Ltd.
,

[1963] 2 All E.R. 575 (H.L.)
, a tort action for negligent misstatement would
have been regarded as incapable of success. The history of our law reveals that
often new developments in the law first surface on motions to strike or similar
preliminary motions, like the one at issue in
Donoghue
v. Stevenson
.
Therefore, on a motion to strike,
it is not determinative that the law has not yet recognized the particular
claim. The court must rather ask whether, assuming the facts pleaded are true,
there is a reasonable prospect that the claim will succeed. The approach must
be generous and err on the side of permitting a novel but arguable claim to
proceed to trial.

[
52
]

While I agree with the plaintiffs that this is the proper lens
through which the court should determine whether a claim based on a new or
novel cause of action should be permitted to proceed to trial, I am not
persuaded that the tort of “Blacklisting”, as framed in the pleadings in this
case, is one that has any chance of success.

[
53
]

Given the elements of this tort that the plaintiffs have proposed,
it is clear that their claim is bound to fail. One reason for reaching this
conclusion is the fact that the plaintiffs have not pleaded that the Ministry
or Province have refused to contract with them. The defendants are correct when
they submit that more is required than simply the fact that the plaintiffs have
not been successful in contracting with the Ministry. There needs to be an
allegation that the defendants, particularly the Province, have refused to
engage the plaintiffs’ services and continue to do so because they have “Blacklisted”
the plaintiffs. This assertion of fact is not explicitly contained in the
pleadings and consequently even if the other facts that are in the pleadings
are deemed to be true, there is still a missing element that the plaintiffs
themselves contend is essential to the claim. As such, I am not persuaded that
the claim based on the proposed tort of “Blacklisting”, as pleaded by the
plaintiffs has any prospect of success.

Is the Plaintiffs’ Claim Unnecessary, Frivolous or an
Abuse of Process?

[
54
]

I have found that none of the four categories that make up the
plaintiffs’ claim have any reasonable prospect of success and are bound to fail
if they went to trial.

[
55
]

For the sake of completeness, I will also add that I find the
plaintiffs’ pleadings run afoul of Rule 9-5(1)(b) and (d). That is, I accept
the defendants’ submission that the plaintiffs’ pleadings and claim as a whole are
unnecessary, frivolous and amount to an abuse of process.

[
56
]

The plaintiffs have not, even after the court gave them a second
opportunity , been able to clearly and concisely articulate an identifiable
factual foundation that would legitimately and appropriate allow the court to
find that some aspect or all of the claim has a reasonable prospect of success
and is not bound to fail. Instead, the plaintiffs have once again filed
pleadings that are prolix and confusing. They are unstructured and in my view
amount to a lengthy narrative that is short on material facts and long on conclusory
statements. In my opinion, the supplementary particulars the plaintiffs attempt
to rely upon do not assist their cause for they are equally prolix and only add
to the nebulousness of their claim.

[
57
]

In my view the plaintiffs’ pleadings are deficient to such a degree
that they transport their claim against the defendants into the realm of the
unnecessary or frivolous. I am also satisfied that to permit the plaintiffs to
prosecute their claim, as it is framed in their pleadings, would result in
unwarranted expenses for the parties, especially the defendants. It would also
result in an unnecessary squandering of judicial resources, especially court
time. These factors lead me to conclude that the plaintiffs’ action as set out
in their pleadings amounts to an abuse of process.

Conclusion

[
58
]

The plaintiffs are obliged to plead in a clear and understandable
fashion the material facts upon which their claim rests. In my opinion they
have not so. Moreover, I find the defendants are correct when they submit that
the material facts pleaded in the amended notice of civil claim do not conform
to Rule 3-1 and 3-7 in that they fail to provide a concise statement of
the material facts that give rise to their claim and they contain conclusions
of law that are not supported by alleged material facts.

[
59
]

In determining this application, I have kept in mind the broad and
liberal approach that the jurisprudence indicates must be used. That includes
erring on the side of permitting a claim to proceed if there is some chance it
might be successful at trial.

[
60
]

In her reasons for judgement on the
defendants’ application to strike out the plaintiffs’ original notice of civil
claim, Master Bouck concluded:

[10]      Similarly,
the NOCC is a defective pleading for many reasons, not the least of which is
that it fails to clearly and concisely define the issues of fact and law to be
decided by the court. The pleading is verbose and confusing. The NOCC is more
akin to a narrative of the evidence that might be presented at a trial,
although not necessarily a trial on the causes of action identified in the
Legal Basis. There are suggestions of a breach of contract claim, but damages
are not being sought by the plaintiffs on that basis. The NOCC improperly
describes the emotions of, or attributes motives to, the individual defendants.
The statement of facts includes conclusions of law and makes legal argument.

[
61
]

In my view the plaintiffs’ pleadings suffer from the same core
deficiencies as were found in their original notice of civil claim. That is,
they are prolix and confusing and do not clearly and fairly identify the
material facts that are essential for the defendants to be able to mount a
defence.

[
62
]

I have considered whether the plaintiffs should be granted another
opportunity to amend their pleadings. In my view that would be pointless. They
were wholly unsuccessful in articulating a justifiable foundation for their
claim in their first notice of civil claim. In my opinion, their second
attempt, supplemented by their response to the defendants’ demand for
particulars, has again failed to meet the necessary elements of proper
pleadings. I am simply not persuaded that the plaintiffs’ pleadings and their
action can be salvaged by granting them a third try at getting things right.

Order

[
63
]

The defendants’ application is granted. Pursuant to Rule 9-5(1), the
plaintiffs’ amended notice of civil claim is struck out and their action is
dismissed as against all of the defendants, including Mr. Otukol.

[
64
]

The defendants are entitled to their ordinary Scale B costs.

“G.R.J.
Gaul J.”
